regenerated retinal ganglion cells can reinnervate specific retinorecipients in the brainstem and that the pattern of axonal ingrowth and the terminal arbors are different in different brainstem nuclei.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new experimental model to study the plasticity of the central nervous system and to develop a new approach for the restoration of visual function in humans with severe retinovascular disease.
the mechanisms underlying the re-establishment and maintenance of the pupillary and visuomotor reflexes in adult animals with peripheral nerve graft links to the brainstem.
the mechanisms that underlie the selective reinnervation of the brainstem by retinal axons after axotomy and transplantation of a peripheral nerve graft in the adult rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adult CNS has the capacity to support the regeneration of retinal axons and that these axons can reinnervate specific target structures in a selective manner.

, in adult rats, retinal axons have the ability to regenerate and reinnervate their original target areas, but the extent of regeneration and reinnervation depends upon the site of entry and the nature of the target area.

the adult central nervous system is able to support the regeneration of retinal ganglion axons and their reinnervation of retinorecipients brainstem targets, although the regrowth of retinal fibers is not as extensive or as precise as that observed in developing animals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the regeneration of retinal axons through peripheral nerve grafts into the brainstem is not only possible in adult rats, but also results in a re-establishment of functional connections.
retinal projections to the brainstem can be re-established in adult animals and that this may have functional consequences for the animal's visual performance.
retinal ganglion cells are capable of regenerating their axons to reestablish a functional retino-recipient connection in the adult brain.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the retina is capable of regenerating to the brainstem after optic nerve transection, and the regenerated retinal axon terminals can form specific synapses within the brainstem nuclei, and this can be achieved in a relatively short period of time (4-13 months).
the brainstem is a highly plastic structure that can be innervated by retinal fibers that have been cut and regenerated in the periphery.

, even though retinal ganglion cells are not able to regenerate to their target in the brain in adult mammals, they are able to regenerate to peripheral nerve grafts and to reinnervate brainstem nuclei in a selective fashion.
